Sandoval County at a glance

Sandoval County is part of the Albuquerque metro area, with 148,834 residents in the 2020 census. Bernalillo is the county seat, and Rio Rancho is the other principal community. The county spans 3,716 square miles, so a sale here might be a suburban lot in Rio Rancho or a larger rural or mountain parcel elsewhere. Where the property sits decides which agencies show up on its tax bill.

Intel's Rio Rancho campus has shaped that market for decades, so sale timing for Rio Rancho owners can follow the local job market.

Treasurer's office

Billing and collection happen in Bernalillo, at 1500 Idalia Road, Building D, NM 87004. Doors are open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The Assessor handles valuation separately.

  • Phone: 505-867-7581 or toll free 1-800-332-8022
  • Email: treasurers@sandovalcountynm.gov
  • Mail: P.O. Box 40, Bernalillo, NM 87004
  • Closed for a staff meeting 2:30 to 3:30 p.m. on the third Wednesday of each month
  • Services and phone payments in English and Spanish
  • During tax season, appointments before 8 a.m. and after 5 p.m. on request at 505-867-7579

You can request a statement of taxes due at any time. Card payments carry a convenience fee, and allow 72 hours for a payment to post.

Where your tax dollar goes

Education takes the largest share. The Treasurer's chart for tax year 2025 splits it this way:

  • Education: 42 percent
  • Municipal government: 21 percent
  • County government: 20 percent
  • State, conservancy and other: 13 percent
  • Contracting hospitals: 5 percent

County programs funded include fire and 911, libraries, public safety, senior programs, roads, the landfill and the detention center. What you personally owe depends on which school district, town and special taxing districts include your lot.

Tax calendar and late charges

The year follows the statewide schedule, and the Treasurer's FAQ lists the dates that matter.

DateWhat happens
January 1Date of assessment; ownership and values are set as of this day
February 28Last day to report value changes, apply for exemptions or remove destroyed property
April 1Assessor mails the Notice of Value
October 1Tax roll goes from the Assessor to the Treasurer
November 1Tax bills mailed; the only bill the owner receives
November 10 to December 10First half due, without penalty through December 10
April 10 to May 10Second half due, without penalty through May 10
June 10Delinquent notices prepared and mailed
July 1Delinquency list for parcels over two years behind goes to the state

Late charges are 1 percent of the base tax per month in interest, plus 1 percent per month in penalty, with a penalty maximum of 5 percent and a minimum of $5. A returned check adds $25 or 5 percent of the check, whichever is greater.

Keeping your tax record correct

Tell the Assessor about changes in writing. An address change must be signed by the owner on record with the Assessor, because bills go to the address on the Assessor's roll and may not be forwarded when you moved over half a year back.

A bill can fail to arrive because an address change came in after printing, a data entry error, or mail lost among the more than 100,000 bills the office sends. A bill can also rise because of a higher assessed value, a lost exemption, a different school district, a higher mil levy or a voter-approved bond.

A clean record speeds up a closing. Before listing or accepting an offer, confirm the owner of record, the mailing address and the status of both halves of the current year, then ask the Treasurer for a statement of taxes due.

Contesting a valuation

Your protest clock starts the day the Notice of Value is mailed and lasts thirty days. The last day of that period is also the final date to claim a family or veteran exemption, to apply for agricultural valuation, to report improvements costing more than $10,000 or to submit a statement of decrease in value.

The petition needs your name and address, a description of the parcel, your reason, and the figure you think is right. The state's protest pamphlet has the details. A county board of three hears the case, owes you a decision inside 180 days, and can be challenged in district court within thirty days after that.

Residential increases are capped as well, at the higher of 103 percent of last year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years back, unless it is a first-year valuation, a new improvement, or follows a sale.

What happens to the tax bill at a sale

Sandoval County has no proration service. The bill follows whoever is the owner on record, and it is mailed even when a lender escrows the payment. Seller and buyer divide the year themselves in the closing paperwork.

  • Sold after October 1? The bill that arrives still shows your name and address.
  • Buyers should send the Assessor a mailing address right after the County Clerk records the deed.
  • A mobile home cannot change title without a tax release, which is paid in certified funds and issued by appointment.
  • Tax liability exists even if a bill was never received, under Section 7-38-36 NMSA 1978.

The State of New Mexico and its counties do not run tax deed, tax certificate or tax lien sales. The only sales are state auctions for parcels with two or more years of delinquent tax. Cash Home Buyers works with Sandoval County owners who want to sell before that point, with no repairs and no commission.

Your closing timeline in Sandoval County

Sandoval County sales move fastest when the paperwork lines up early. Here is a sensible order.

  1. Call the Treasurer for a statement of taxes due, which covers both halves of the current year and anything older.
  2. Check with the Assessor that the owner of record and mailing address are right, and report any change in writing.
  3. Tell the title company about any protest or exemption on file so the closing statement matches the county record.
  4. Decide with the buyer how the year's tax is split, since the Treasurer does not do it for you.
  5. After closing, make sure the buyer gets a mailing address to the Assessor so the next November bill finds the right person.

A cash sale skips the lender's review, so the main limit on speed is how quickly the tax balance and title are cleared. Bring a copy of your deed, a photo ID and your latest tax bill to any meeting with the title company, and keep the Treasurer's statement of taxes due with your closing papers. If your property is a mobile home, book the tax release appointment early, because releases are scheduled rather than walk-in.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Sandoval County Treasurer's office?

It is at 1500 Idalia Road, Building D, in Bernalillo, NM 87004, on the first floor. Call 505-867-7581 or 1-800-332-8022, or write to P.O. Box 40, Bernalillo, NM 87004.

When are Sandoval County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10 and is paid without penalty through December 10. The second half is due April 10 and is paid without penalty through May 10.

What are the late fees on Sandoval County property tax?

Interest is 1 percent of the base tax per month. The penalty is also 1 percent per month, capped at 5 percent, with a $5 minimum.

Does the county prorate property tax when I sell?

No. The county offers no proration. Sellers and buyers split the year in their closing paperwork.

Can Sandoval County sell my house for unpaid tax?

Not the county itself. Only the state holds auctions, for parcels two or more years behind, and the Treasurer passes the delinquency list to the state on July 1.

Eddy County at a glance

Eddy County occupies New Mexico's southeast corner, up against Texas. Carlsbad is the county seat, Artesia is the other city, and Hope and Loving are villages. The 2020 census counted 62,314 residents: 32,238 in Carlsbad, 12,875 in Artesia, 1,390 in Loving and 15,811 in the rest of the county.

About a quarter of residents live outside any incorporated place, and a rural house is taxed by a different mix of districts than one inside Carlsbad or Artesia. Oil and gas, potash, the federal Waste Isolation Pilot Plant and tourism drive local jobs, so housing demand can swing with drilling and plant schedules. Workers on short assignments often rent, which is why many Eddy County owners end up as landlords.

Who values property and who collects

The Eddy County Assessor values property. The Eddy County Treasurer bills and collects. Under state law the county assessor does the valuing, with these exceptions: railroads, pipelines, utilities, airlines, power plants and mineral property, all valued by the state Taxation and Revenue Department. In oil country that carve-out is big: 531 properties statewide, worth $32 billion and about 17 percent of the tax base, are valued by the state.

OfficeWhat it doesAddress or phone
Eddy County TreasurerSends bills, takes payments101 W. Greene St., Suite 117, Carlsbad, NM 88220; (575) 885-3913
Eddy County AssessorSets values, takes exemption claims and protests(575) 885-3813
Point and Pay portalOnline payment by bill searchLinked from the county site

Current hours are on the county's treasurer and assessor pages, worth a look before you drive over.

Due dates

Your bill should arrive by November 1. Pay half by November 10 and half by April 10 of the next year. Interest waits until December 10 for the first half and May 10 for the second.

Property is valued as of January 1. The state fixes rates near September 1.

Unpaid property tax is no ordinary debt. Starting each January 1 it attaches to the real property as a first lien, outranking every other interest, recorded or not. Nobody has to file anything for it to exist, so a search of recorded documents will miss it. Ask the treasurer for today's balance before you list or accept an offer.

How valuation works and what changes at sale

As long as one owner keeps a home, its taxable residential value climbs by at most 3 percent a year. The exact ceiling is whichever is higher: 103 percent of last year's figure, or 106.1 percent of the figure from two years ago. A sale resets it, as do a first valuation year, new improvements and a change of use or zoning.

One third of assessed value is taxable, and rates are set only after yield control adjusts them.

In practice, the buyer's first-year value is reset to current market value, so the new owner may pay more than you did. After decades of ownership, expect questions about that jump. The $2,000 head of family exemption protects a resident's primary home and falls away on a sale, which means the buyer has to claim it again.

  • A transfer to your spouse, or to a child living in the home, is one of the listed exceptions to "change of ownership."
  • Moving the house into a revocable trust for yourself, a spouse or a child is excepted as well.
  • Deeding the house to an LLC you own does count as a change of ownership, a New Mexico Court of Appeals decision held.

How to protest your valuation

Write out your protest and deliver it to the county assessor. The deadline is April 1 or 30 days after the notice of valuation was mailed, whichever is later. The county valuation protest board decides it, and a state Taxation and Revenue appraiser holds one of its seats.

Filing on time keeps the disputed portion from going delinquent. The alternative is paying up front and asking district court for a refund by January 10 of the next year.

The state's protest pamphlet lists the statute citations.

If the tax goes unpaid

Interest begins once the December 10 and May 10 dates pass. When a third full year of delinquency ends, the state takes over the account. Its Delinquent Property Tax Bureau tries phone calls, certified letters, visits to the property and posted notices, and it will set up installment agreements. Public auction is the last resort, and every county must hold one each calendar year.

An auction pays off the tax, penalty, interest and costs first, and whatever is left goes to the former owner. That is a poor way to part with a house you could have sold.

  • An inherited home may still get bills addressed to the person who died.
  • Absentee owners of rural parcels can miss notices that go to an old address.

Before a cash sale

Pull together three things: the treasurer's balance, the assessor's record of who holds the land and the minerals, and the clerk's recorded documents. An unrecorded deed or mortgage does not bind a later purchaser in New Mexico, so recording is not optional.

Insist that offers come in writing, learn who covers recording and title costs, and compare the figure to your payoff and tax due.

A cash sale has no lender appraisal or underwriting in the way, so timing depends on how fast the title company clears the lien and records the deed. Keep the tax balance and a copy of your deed handy. If you hold mineral rights, tell the title company early, since the land and the minerals may have different owners of record.

A plan for selling in Eddy County

Listing with an agent or selling for cash, you do the same groundwork whether the house is in Carlsbad, Artesia or out in the country.

  1. Call the treasurer at (575) 885-3913 and request the balance for each year. Years in delinquency are the ones that can reach the state.
  2. Ring the assessor at (575) 885-3813 to learn if the head of family exemption sits on your account and if any protest is still open.
  3. Check who is named as owner of the land and of any minerals, and make sure your deed is recorded.
  4. Hand the payoff figures to the title company. It will settle the lien from your proceeds and deliver clean title.
  5. Warn the buyer that the exemption ends at sale, which makes the first bill under new ownership look different.

Owners who rented the house to workers on short assignments should also gather lease papers and tell the buyer about any tenant who is staying.

Frequently asked questions

When is Eddy County property tax due?

Half comes due November 10 and the rest April 10. You have until December 10 and May 10, respectively, before interest starts.

Who do I call about my Eddy County property tax bill?

The Eddy County Treasurer, at (575) 885-3913, handles bills and payments from 101 W. Greene St., Suite 117, in Carlsbad. Call the Assessor at (575) 885-3813 for valuations and exemptions.

How much can my Eddy County home value increase each year?

The limit is the higher of 103 percent of last year's value or 106.1 percent of the figure from two years back. When ownership changes, the limit resets.

Is there a New Mexico estate or inheritance tax on an Eddy County house?

No. The state's estate tax ended as of January 1, 2005, and there is no inheritance tax. Only very large estates can still owe federal estate tax.

Can I sell an Eddy County house with property tax owed?

Yes, but the lien dates from January 1 and outranks other interests, so it must be paid or settled before the buyer gets clean title. Start with a payoff from the treasurer.

Who runs property tax in Bernalillo County

The work is divided between two elected offices that share Alvarado Square, 415 Silver Ave SW in Albuquerque, the county seat. One decides what your property is worth and builds the roll, and the other sends bills and takes money. The Assessor's number is (505) 222-3700 and the Treasurer's is (505) 468-7031.

Bernalillo County is New Mexico's most populous, with more than 676,000 residents, about 106,000 of them outside city limits in Albuquerque, Los Ranchos and Tijeras. Parcels run from city lots to unincorporated land, and the rate you pay hinges on the districts around your address.

The Assessor's job covers real property, business personal property, livestock and manufactured homes. It notifies owners of value and hands the finished roll to the Treasurer.

The property tax year

Value is fixed on January 1, notices go out by April 1, rates are set in September, the roll reaches the Treasurer by October 1, and bills are in the mail by early November.

EventTimingOffice
Property valued as of its conditionJanuary 1Assessor
Exemption and Head of Family applicationsEnd of February, or a month after the Notice of ValueAssessor
Notices of Value mailedBy April 1Assessor
Valuation certified to the stateJune 15Assessor
Delinquent notices mailedAbout June 10Treasurer
Rates setSeptemberState Dept. of Finance and Administration
Tax roll deliveredOctober 1Assessor to Treasurer
Bills mailed, first half dueNovember 1 and November 10Treasurer
Second half dueApril 10Treasurer

If November 1 lands on a weekend, bills go out the next business day. Anyone who is not on the 10-month payment agreement pays in one lump or in two installments.

How the tax is calculated

Take one-third of assessed value to get taxable value. Subtract exemptions from it, and only then apply the mill rate. What remains is net taxable value, after items like Head of Family and the veteran exemption.

The state sets mill rates, and they differ by taxing district. The Treasurer posts rate charts for 2016 to 2025, and the Assessor's property search shows the figures for one address. In the latest cycle many rates fell, but rising valuations, a new taxing district and added tax initiatives still pushed bills up across the county.

Statewide, residential taxable value may grow at most 3% a year. That ceiling covers assessment growth, and the mill rate is a separate matter.

Exemptions and the value freeze

The Assessor handles Head of Family, veteran and disabled veteran exemptions, plus a value freeze. You do not file a protest form for any of them.

  • Head of Family takes $2,000 off taxable value for one property per household in the state.
  • The veteran exemption takes up to $10,000 off taxable value with a certificate from the state's veteran service commission. Once granted, it stays on the record.
  • A disabled veteran can exempt a share of the primary residence that matches the VA disability rating.
  • The value freeze serves owners aged 65 and over whose modified gross income is $42,900 or under, and disabled owners at $41,900 or under. It halts the 3% assessment increase but leaves the tax rate alone.

The deadline is a month after the Notice of Value goes out. The Assessor's tax savings page has the forms. A value freeze never forces you to sell at the frozen value.

How to appeal your valuation

Your protest goes to the Assessor, either through the online appeal portal or in person at 415 Silver Ave SW, and it must arrive within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing. You then sit down informally with a field appraiser. If you and the appraiser still disagree, the Protest Valuation Review Board hears the matter. An amended Notice of Value restarts the 30 days from its own mailing date.

Business personal property, manufactured home and livestock protests run on a separate spring window, so check the Assessor's protest page each year.

If the window has closed, the fallback is paying in full and filing a refund claim at the Second Judicial District Court, 400 Lomas Blvd NW. The Treasurer puts the cutoff 60 days after the first installment due date. Payment comes first. The Assessor lists a $132 court filing fee. Call the court self-help center at 505-841-6702 to confirm the cutoff before you rely on it.

With a protest still open in December, pay the first half on the original bill, as the Treasurer advises. If you win, a new bill and a refund follow. If you lose, you have avoided late fees.

Due dates and late penalties

A late payment draws interest of 1% a month and, on top, a penalty of 1% a month that stops at 5% and never drops below $5. The clock starts December 10 for the first half and May 10 for the second.

You can pay in person on the first floor of 415 Silver Ave SW, online through the county's payment vendor, or by mail to PO Box 27800, Albuquerque, NM 87125-7800. The Treasurer warns against bank bill-pay services because of mailing delays, misrouting and no confirmation. Owners are liable even if a bill never arrives. About 10,600 bills came back undelivered in the 2025 cycle, mostly for outdated addresses, so keep your mailing address current.

Delinquent notices go out around June 10.

Selling with taxes owed

The January 1 owner owes that year's tax. A manufactured home additionally requires a tax release before it can be sold, moved or traded. The title company looks up what is due and settles it from your proceeds.

A manufactured home owner gets the tax release from the Treasurer, showing current and prior years paid, and starts the process at the Assessor with proof of ownership. Land and a manufactured home on it get separate notices and bills unless the home has been converted to real property. Public improvement district charges transfer to the buyer, and a seller can prepay the balance.

Our Bernalillo County Clerk guide explains the residential transfer affidavit that the Assessor expects after closing. Some owners carrying back taxes, an inherited house or a tenant pick an as-is cash sale so they can skip repairs and showings. The tax still gets paid from the proceeds.

Ahead of listing, get the balance from the Treasurer, an exemption check from the Assessor, and a heads-up to the title company about any open protest.

Preparing to sell in Bernalillo County

A little groundwork saves days at closing. Begin by collecting the Treasurer's figures for both halves of this year, and ask the Assessor which exemptions are attached to the parcel. Tell your title company whether a protest is open, because a pending case can change the figure the buyer's side expects.

Keep your mailing address current. About 10,600 bills came back undelivered in the 2025 cycle, so an old address is common and avoidable. If your home was inherited or has a tenant, collect any estate or lease papers before you list, because the title company is going to request them.

Selling as-is for cash is an option for owners who would rather avoid repairs and showings. What the county is owed stays the same, so the payoff steps do not change.

Frequently asked questions

When are Bernalillo County property taxes due?

Plan on November 10 for the first half and April 10 for the second. Late fees start December 10 and May 10.

Who sets property values in Bernalillo County?

The elected County Assessor sets values and mails Notices of Value by April 1. The elected Treasurer sends bills and collects. Each September the state fixes the mill rates.

How do I protest my Bernalillo County valuation?

Submit a protest form to the Assessor online or at 415 Silver Ave SW, no more than 30 days after the Notice of Value is mailed. An informal meeting comes first, then a Protest Valuation Review Board hearing if needed.

Can I sell a Bernalillo County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The title company ordinarily pays the balance, penalty and interest included, from your closing proceeds. Confirm the figure with the Treasurer at (505) 468-7031.

Does Bernalillo County send a bill if a mortgage company pays my taxes?

Yes. Every owner gets a bill even if a lender pays it. The bill names the mortgage company that requested the amount, and you are still the one who has to confirm it was paid.

San Juan County basics

San Juan County fills the northwest corner of New Mexico, with Aztec as the county seat. Its 2020 census population was 121,661, and it is part of the Farmington metropolitan area. The Navajo Nation covers 60.45 percent of the county's area, so much of the county lies outside the ordinary city lots of Farmington, Aztec and Bloomfield.

Other communities include Kirtland, Flora Vista, Fruitland, Waterflow, Shiprock, Lee Acres, Navajo Dam and Nenahnezad. The bill depends on the school district, city and voter-approved bonds covering a property, so where the house sits changes what the owner pays. Energy, health care and education supply most of the jobs, which means demand for homes tends to follow the oil and gas cycle.

How the tax is calculated

Taxable value is one third of full value, and the rate is applied to that amount. A county appraiser sets full value, the Assessor assembles the tax roll, and the rate is quoted in dollars per thousand.

The rate comes from outside the county offices. The State Department of Finance and Administration sets it every year from budgets submitted by schools, cities and voters through approved bond issues, and certifies it each September. The Treasurer sends a reminder on April 1 to owners with a balance from earlier years, and a delinquent notice after the second-half due date. Three or more years of back taxes can put a property on the State of New Mexico's auction list.

Exemptions and limits

Three programs come up most often: head of family, the veteran exemption and the value freeze for some older or disabled owners. Head of family is $2,000 off taxable value, covers residential property only, and renews on its own once claimed.

For the veteran exemption, an honorably discharged veteran living in New Mexico brings a certificate of eligibility from the county veteran service office to the Assessor in person between January 1 and April 30. A disabled veteran's occupied principal residence can be exempt in an amount equal to the federal disability percentage. The county lists that office at 1800 E. 30th St., Farmington.

The limit on value increases covers a single-family dwelling owned and occupied by someone 65 or older, or disabled, whose income stays under an inflation-adjusted limit. You must apply, and apply again each year for three years.

State law also caps residential value growth. Under Section 7-36-21.2, the value may not exceed the higher of 103 percent of the prior year or 106.1 percent of two years earlier. A change of ownership in the prior year lifts that cap for the following tax year. The state's protest pamphlet has the statute text.

How to protest a valuation

Visit the Assessor first. Talk to an appraiser in person, and if you still disagree, request a protest packet. You have thirty days from the mailing date of the Notice of Value to file with the County Valuation Protest Board through the Assessor's office.

The Assessor notifies you by certified mail at least fifteen days before the hearing. State law puts the burden of proving the value wrong on the owner, so bring evidence: recent comparable sales, a repair estimate, photographs of damage or a recent appraisal.

A Notice of Value is not a tax bill. If the value, mailing address and property description are right, no action is needed.

Before you sell

Three things trip up sellers: the mobile home release, the river-flood paperwork and the state auction rule. A mobile home tax release is required for a duplicate title, a title change and a moving permit. The Treasurer charges $5 for a regular release and $25 for a moving permit, and takes certified funds only, with no personal or business checks.

Unpaid mobile home and personal property tax follows its own path. A Pre-Demand Warrant gives ten business days to pay or arrange payment. After that, a Demand Warrant is served by a deputy sheriff with a $42 fee for each delivery.

If your property sits near the San Juan or Animas rivers, keep damage records and insurance claim papers together, since both affect what a buyer will pay.

For real estate, the State Property Tax Division auctions long-delinquent parcels as is, with no right of redemption. Cash Home Buyers speaks with San Juan County owners who would rather close on their own timeline than wait for that.

Practical order: get the Treasurer's balance for every year, confirm the exemptions on file with the Assessor, and give both to your title company before the buyer's deadline.

A seller's checklist for San Juan County

Property near Farmington, Aztec or Bloomfield sells under the same county rules as land on the edge of the reservation, but the paperwork can differ, so start by learning what you own.

  1. Request the Treasurer's balance for every year, and note whether the November 10 and April 10 halves are both paid.
  2. Ask the Assessor whether head of family, a veteran exemption or the value freeze is on file. Any of them may need to be reclaimed by the buyer.
  3. For a mobile home, order the tax release early, and bring certified funds, because the county takes no personal or business checks.
  4. Pass the figures to the title company so it can pay the Treasurer at closing.

Keep the Notice of Value, the latest bill and any protest papers together. Buyers and title companies ask for all three.

Frequently asked questions

When is San Juan County, NM property tax due?

The first half and full amount are due November 10, and the second half is due April 10. Penalty and interest start December 11 on the first half and May 11 on the second.

Where do I pay San Juan County property tax?

The Treasurer's office is at 100 S. Oliver Dr., Suite 300, in Aztec. You can also pay by mail, at the drop box on the east side of the administration building, or online through the county's portal.

How long do I have to file a protest in San Juan County?

You have thirty days from the date the Notice of Value was mailed. File through the Assessor's office with the County Valuation Protest Board; the owner carries the burden of showing the value is wrong.

How much is the head of family exemption in San Juan County?

It is $2,000, deducted from taxable value on residential property only. After you sign up, it renews automatically each year.

What happens after three years of unpaid property tax in San Juan County?

The property can be added to the auction list kept by the State of New Mexico. Failure to pay three or more years of back taxes could lead to that.

About the county

Doña Ana County is in the south of New Mexico along the Texas and Mexico borders. It has more than 219,500 residents and includes the cities of Anthony, Las Cruces and Sunland Park, the Town of Mesilla and the Village of Hatch.

Las Cruces, the county seat, is the biggest city in southern New Mexico (111,385 people in 2020) and the hub of the Mesilla Valley, a farming area on the Rio Grande floodplain.

Sellers here may hold a Las Cruces city lot, an irrigated farm parcel or open desert acreage, all under one tax office. Each one is taxed at a rate built from the city, schools and special districts covering it.

Who handles property tax

Valuation is the Doña Ana County Assessor's job, and billing and collecting belong to the Doña Ana County Treasurer. The Assessor does not tax anything.

The state sets every taxing entity's rate, called the mill levy, through its Department of Finance and Administration. Cities, school districts and other bodies draw their share based on what they budget.

Multiply taxable value, less exemptions, by the mill rate. One-third of assessed value counts as taxable. Your own district's rate is posted on the Assessor's site.

Tax dates

Two payments make up the year. November 10 is the first-half due date, and December 10 is the last day before that half is delinquent. April 10 and May 10 play the same roles for the second half.

January 1Property valued; liens attach to delinquent real and personal property

What late payment costs

Each month the balance sits unpaid, interest of 1% of the base tax is added, along with a 1% penalty that can build for up to five months, never below $5. A bounced check costs $25.

No law allows a county treasurer to waive penalty or interest, and nobody else can erase them once they accrue. A bill that never shows up does not excuse you, because the obligation to pay stands either way.

The consequences escalate over time:

  • Every June, the Treasurer mails a notice on any bill that is 30 or more days delinquent.
  • Delinquent taxes are transferred to the state's Property Tax Division on July 1.
  • Real property two years past its delinquency date can go to a state public auction.
  • With three or more prior years owing, the property is sold unless every year is paid in full before the sale.
  • Manufactured homes and personal property may be seized and sold after six months.

If you cannot pay everything, the state Property Tax Division may offer an installment agreement that halts a sale.

How to protest or reduce your bill

Send the County Assessor a valuation protest within 30 days of the date printed on the Notice of Value, typically in April. Miss that and your remaining path is paying everything by December 10, then asking District Court for a refund by January 10.

A pending protest does not suspend payment. Pay at least the tax on the undisputed value when the half comes due: December 10 and May 10. If a protest results in a corrected bill, it carries a new delinquency date and arrives at least 30 days before payment is due, without interest or penalty on the amended amount.

There is no homestead exemption in New Mexico. Relief comes in three forms:

  • Head of Family, for a resident whose primary residence it is. You apply once and it continues, one per household.
  • A veteran exemption, which requires a certificate from the state's veteran service commission, taken to the Assessor during the Notice of Value period.
  • A valuation freeze, available to owners who are 65 or older or disabled with modified gross income under $35,000. You apply three years running, and after that it holds for as long as you live in the home.

Check the current income limit with the Assessor first.

Selling with taxes owed

The January 1 owner of record answers for that year's tax. A lien remains on the property whoever owns it next. The Treasurer cites section 7-37-7 NMSA 1978 for this rule.

Prorating is not something the county does. If buyer and seller want to share the year, the sale contract and the title company's closing statement have to say so. If the property is mortgaged, make sure the lender has paid. The county does not mail an escrowed bill to the owner, though you can request one.

Special situations to watch:

  • Before a mobile home's title can transfer, or a moving permit issue, the Assessor must give a property tax release, and personal checks do not work for that payment.
  • Splitting or combining land requires all taxes paid, current year included, before the Treasurer issues a Certification of Taxes Paid.
  • A closed business still owes tax for the year if it operated on January 1.

Farm parcels, inherited land and years of back tax lead many owners to an as-is cash sale, where the tax is paid out of the sale money.

A workable order: get the Treasurer's payoff, check exemptions with the Assessor, and give both numbers to your closing agent. Bring your deed too. If you plan to split farm acreage, say so before you sign anything.

Preparing a Doña Ana County sale

Doña Ana sales usually go smoother when the tax picture is clear before the first showing. The steps below suit most owners.

  1. Request the Treasurer's balance for each year, not just this one. Older years are the ones that move a parcel toward the state list.
  2. Confirm with the Assessor that Head of Family or the veteran exemption is on the record, and note the Notice of Value date in case a protest is still possible.
  3. If the land is farm acreage or part of a larger tract, find out whether a split is planned, since the Treasurer certifies taxes paid only after everything owed is cleared.
  4. Give the closing agent your deed and the payoff numbers, and the year can be divided fairly between you and the buyer.
  5. With a lender escrow, verify that the lender actually paid. No escrowed bill is mailed to you unless you request it.

With no lender appraisal to wait on, a cash as-is closing is paced mainly by how quickly the tax balance and title clear.

Frequently asked questions

When are Doña Ana County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10, and it turns delinquent once December 10 passes. April 10 is the second-half date, with delinquency starting after May 10.

How much are late fees in Doña Ana County?

Each month adds 1% of the base tax in interest, and a 1% penalty builds for up to five months, with a $5 floor. Neither can be waived.

Can Doña Ana County property taxes be prorated?

No. Buyer and seller handle any sharing of the tax in their contract and at closing.

How long do I have to protest my Doña Ana County valuation?

Thirty days from the date on the Notice of Value, which typically falls in April. Later, a refund claim means paying in full and filing in District Court by January 10.

What happens if I do not pay Doña Ana County property tax?

On July 1, delinquent taxes are handed to the state Property Tax Division. Real property can then go to state auction after two unpaid years, or sooner with three or more years owing.

Socorro County at a glance

Socorro County sprawls across central New Mexico, and the city of Socorro is the seat. Roughly 6,649 square miles hold 16,595 people (2020 count), 8,707 of them in the city. Magdalena, San Antonio, Lemitar, Polvadera and Veguita are the other named communities.

Property type varies a great deal. You might own a town lot, a small river-valley place or a big tract far from pavement, and the assessor prices each by what it is and how it is used. Distant land tends to linger on the market, which is worth weighing if your deadline is firm.

Offices to know

The county splits the work between two elected offices. Values come from the Assessor and payments go to the Treasurer. A delinquent account eventually moves to the State Property Tax Division.

  • Assessor: PO Box J, 200 Church St, Socorro, NM 87801, phone 575-835-0714. Values homes, businesses and other taxable property, then passes the rolls on for billing.
  • Treasurer: PO Box KK, 200 Church St, Socorro, NM 87801, phone 575-835-1701. Weekday hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with federal holidays off.
  • State Property Tax Division: Manuel Lujan Building, 1200 S. St. Francis Drive, Santa Fe.

County staff stay out of real estate deals. They neither broker nor advise on sales, so take closing questions to a title company or an attorney.

Valuation and protests

By April 1, each owner is mailed a Notice of Valuation, the document that sets the value behind your bill. Taxable value works out to a third of appraised value, minus exemptions you qualify for, among them head of household and a veteran exemption.

Grounds for a protest include the assessor's value or classification, how value is divided among taxing units, a refused exemption, or a cap on an increase. Under Section 7-38-24 you file the petition with the assessor, generally within 30 days of the mailing date. If the notice was sent along with last year's tax bill, the deadline is the later of April 1 and 30 days after mailing.

Pull together the notice, a recent bill and whatever backs up a lower number, for instance contractor quotes or damage photos. The assessor's line, 575-835-0714, can supply the petition form and confirm the current date.

A 2026 bill, House Bill 285, changed the disabled veteran exemption. How a sale unfolds

The calendar is short, which makes it easy to track. Notices of Valuation arrive by April 1. The second-half payment falls due April 10. Sellers should note them: a spring or late-fall closing sits close to a payment date, and the title company must divide that bill between you and the buyer.

If a closing straddles a payment date, find out in advance who pays that half. Ask the title company to show the split on the settlement statement, so nothing is left to memory. The Treasurer's office can confirm what has already been paid for the year.

Otero County overview

In south-central New Mexico, on the Texas border, Otero County has one city: Alamogordo, the county seat. Cloudcroft and Tularosa are villages. Smaller places include Boles Acres, High Rolls, La Luz, Mayhill, Mescalero, Orogrande, Timberon and Holloman AFB. The 2020 census counted 67,839 people.

Holloman Air Force Base employs the most people, with tourism around Cloudcroft, the Mescalero resort and White Sands National Park next. Some owners arrive for a fixed tour at the base and must leave on a set date, which leaves little room to handle repairs, a tax bill or a listing.

Property tax offices

Property tax runs through two county offices at the same Alamogordo address. Finding, listing and valuing property is the Assessor's task, while the Treasurer sends out the bill and receives payment. Take a disputed value to the Assessor, and a payoff question to the Treasurer.

Each county office has searchable online records. The Treasurer's EagleWeb portal displays balances, and the Assessor's portal displays current ownership.

Due dates and how to pay

Otero County splits the year into two installments. The first half is payable by November 10 and late once December 10 passes. April 10 is the second-half deadline, late after May 10.

The Treasurer's office accepts payment at the counter, by mail, over the web or on the phone. The county's pay-by-phone page gives 1-877-707-1126, or 575-437-2030 and option 2. Credit cards run 2.39 percent with a $1.95 floor, while debit cards run $3.95.

  • November 10: pay the first installment
  • December 10: last penalty-free day for it
  • April 10: pay the second installment
  • May 10: last penalty-free day for that one

Owing does not depend on receiving. If the mail never brings your bill, the tax is still due, so tell the Assessor whenever your address changes.

Valuation, the cap and protests

The Assessor sets the value, and contesting it has a 30-day clock. Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978 sends the petition to the county assessor, due on April 1 or thirty days after the valuation notice is mailed, whichever comes later. It names the owner and property, explains the error and gives the figure you think is right.

A valuation protests board of three voting members hears each case and must rule within 180 days of filing. If you disagree with its ruling, district court is open to you for thirty days after the order.

There is also a ceiling on taxable home values. Under Section 7-36-21.2, a residential value cannot pass the greater of 103 percent of last year's figure or 106.1 percent of the figure from two years ago. The ceiling does not cover first-year valuations, last year's improvements, or the year after a sale or rezoning.

The sale exception is the one to remember. A buyer may see a higher assessed value the year after closing, so your old bill will not tell you what the new owner pays.

If the tax goes unpaid

Penalty and interest come first, and after enough years a state auction can follow. The Property Tax Division runs these sales, not the county. Bidding starts at taxes, penalty, interest and costs, and a sale is held only after title research is done and other collection steps are used up. Not every one of the 33 counties has an auction each year.

Only the tax lien is wiped out by a tax sale. Other liens survive. What the buyer receives is a tax deed, which acts like a quitclaim and carries no title warranty. Former owners cannot redeem in New Mexico, but Section 7-38-70 allows a two-year court challenge.

With several years of tax behind on an Otero County house, move early. A sale before the property lands on an auction list leaves the equity in your hands.

Selling with taxes owed

Three things matter most: a current payoff, a clean record of ownership and a plan for both installments. The Treasurer supplies the balance, and the title or escrow company wants it before closing.

  • Look up the balance on the Treasurer's portal and confirm each half of this year.
  • Scan for older years too. Long-delinquent tax is what pushes a property toward auction.
  • Check the mailing address on the tax roll. Both the notice of value and the bill are sent there.
  • With a mobile home, ask the Assessor about a tax release before you try to move the title.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in this position, among them heirs of a house with tax behind it and owners who moved away. We buy as-is, so a stale tax bill, a half-done repair or a tenant need not be sorted out beforehand. Before you talk to any buyer, collect your deed, the newest bill and the Treasurer's payoff, so every offer can be weighed against what you truly owe.

A seller's order of work in Otero County

Military postings, inheritances and moves out of state all put owners under time pressure. Working in the right order keeps a short timeline from turning into a mistake.

  1. Start in the Assessor's portal and make sure the owner of record and the property description are correct. Errors here slow every later step.
  2. Open the Treasurer's portal, or call 575-437-2030, and note what is owed for each year.
  3. Look at your Notice of Value. If the number seems high and the protest window is still open, an informal talk with the Assessor costs nothing.
  4. Send the payoff to the title or escrow office, which will pay the Treasurer out of your closing money.
  5. Give the buyer a forwarding address for any bill that lands after the sale, and tell the Assessor too.

If you must be gone by a certain date, mention it at the start. Cash buyers can often adapt to a tight schedule, while a financed sale depends on an appraisal and lender review that you do not control. Either way, keep copies of every notice from the Assessor and the Treasurer in one folder, because the title company may ask for any of them on short notice.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Otero County property tax?

Go to the Otero County Treasurer at 1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310, or call 575-437-2030. Online and phone payments are also accepted, the phone number being 1-877-707-1126.

When is the first half of Otero County property tax due?

November 10 is the first-half due date, with delinquency after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and goes delinquent after May 10.

How long do I have to protest my Otero County valuation?

Whichever comes later, April 1 or thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. Send the Otero County Assessor a petition giving your reason and your figure.

Can the county sell my house at auction for unpaid tax?

Only the state auctions property after long delinquency. Sales by the Property Tax Division are as is, at a floor of the taxes, penalty, interest and costs, with no right of redemption.

Can I sell an Otero County house that has tax due?

Yes. The title company asks the Treasurer for a payoff, and the balance is taken from your proceeds at closing. Selling before the auction list avoids that outcome.

San Miguel County overview

San Miguel County is a long, narrow county in northeastern New Mexico that runs from the Great Plains to the Rocky Mountains. The only city, and the county seat, is Las Vegas. The 2020 census found 27,201 residents spread over 4,736 square miles. Pecos and part of Mosquero are villages, and smaller communities include Sapello, Rociada, Montezuma, Ilfeld, San Miguel del Vado and Tererro.

Places are small and far apart. A house in Sapello or Rociada is a long way from services in Las Vegas, so sellers out there should be ready for buyers' questions about road access, utilities and boundary lines before any price is agreed.

Property tax offices

The Assessor and the Treasurer share a building and work in sequence. The Assessor values property and builds the tax roll, then hands it to the Treasurer in the fall.

OfficeAddressPhone
San Miguel County Assessor500 W. National Ave., Suite 105, Las Vegas, NM 87701505-454-1430
San Miguel County Treasurer500 W. National Ave., Suite 111, Las Vegas, NM 87701505-425-9376
NM Property Tax Division (state auctions)Santa Fe505-827-0883

Walk-in hours at both county offices are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Treasurer also accepts online payment through a bill-pay site and by phone at 877-690-3729 using Jurisdiction #4115. If online payment gives you trouble, call 505-425-9377 so the payment is not doubled.

Due dates

Pay the first half by November 10 or it turns delinquent on December 11. Pay the second half by April 10 or it turns delinquent on May 11. After that, late fees land on the 11th of every month against what is still owed, even when you have made partial payments.

Property is auctioned by the state in the third year of delinquency, and the Treasurer can take payments on an account only until it is placed on the state's list.

The Assessor's yearly calendar runs on its own track: an assessment period from January 1 to February 28, tax rates entered on September 1, the tax roll going to the Treasurer on October 1, and a mass year rollover starting December 1. Notices of Valuation are dated June 1, but the date printed on your own notice is the one that sets your deadline.

Tax auction

The state posts San Miguel County auctions on its calendar, usually starting at 10:00 a.m. People who want to bid register from 8 a.m. until the sale begins. The Taxation and Revenue Department's auction page links to the advertisement and to registration.

Everything sells as is and refunds are not given. Bidding opens at the taxes, penalty, interest and costs owed. The winner receives a tax deed, which is the same as a quitclaim deed, and only the tax lien is cleared. Any other lien on the property stays.

The County Treasurer or Assessor can give you the sale list. Redemption does not exist in New Mexico, though Section 7-38-70 allows a two-year court challenge to a sale. That remedy is narrow. Paying the balance, or selling the house, before the sale is much safer.

How to protest a valuation

Protests go to the Assessor in writing. Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978 sets the deadline at April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed, whichever is later. State your name and address, describe the property, and say why the value is off and what it should be. The state's protest pamphlet reprints the statute.

The Assessor's page offers a protest petition and pamphlet in English and Spanish. Staff are reappraising across the county, and appraisers carry county identification and wear safety vests, so a visit from one is not unusual.

Three board members at the county valuation protests board decide each protest within 180 days, and district court takes appeals filed within thirty days. Separately, residential value may rise only to the greater of 103 percent of last year or 106.1 percent of two years back, except after a sale or new improvements.

Selling with taxes owed

Identify each unpaid year, confirm the parcel is not already on the state's list, and get a payoff figure to the title company. The county does not prorate property tax, so the closing paperwork splits the year between you and the buyer. For a mid-year sale, check with the Treasurer on how it is handled.

  • Call the Treasurer at 505-425-9376 for the balance on each year.
  • Find out whether the parcel is on the state's current delinquent list.
  • Check the Assessor's records for the owner of record, especially on inherited land passed through a family without a recorded deed.
  • Selling a mobile home along with the land? Ask the Assessor if a tax release is required.

Before listing a San Miguel County property

Distance and old paperwork are the usual causes of delay in this county, more than tax rules. A few steps taken early help.

  1. Walk the property lines or locate the survey. Buyers for land in Sapello, Rociada or Tererro often ask where the boundaries sit.
  2. Confirm how access works, including the road and any shared lane, and which utilities serve the house.
  3. Ask the Assessor who is the owner of record. If land passed through a family without a recorded deed, fix that before any contract is signed.
  4. Collect the Treasurer's balance for all years, and note the 11th-of-the-month fee schedule if anything is past due.
  5. Give the title company all of it at once, so one call produces the payoff and a clear list of what is left to do.

Selling for cash as-is takes away most of the repair and showing work, though the title and tax steps are identical to those in a regular sale.

Papers to have in hand

When you meet a buyer or the title company, bring a copy of your deed, the most recent tax bill and any Notice of Valuation you received. If you filed a protest, bring that petition and any reply from the Assessor. For inherited property, bring whatever shows how title passed to you, whether a deed, a court order or an affidavit, because the Assessor's records may still show an earlier owner.

If you are not sure which year a payment was applied to, call the Treasurer at 505-425-9376 and ask for a statement by year. Keep that statement with your closing file.

Frequently asked questions

Where are the San Miguel County tax offices?

Both the Treasurer and the Assessor are at 500 W. National Ave. in Las Vegas, NM 87701. The Treasurer is in Suite 111 and the Assessor in Suite 105.

When are San Miguel County property taxes due?

November 10 is the first-half due date, with delinquency on December 11. April 10 is the second-half date, with delinquency on May 11. Late fees keep adding on the 11th of each month to past due balances.

When does San Miguel County property go to tax auction?

In the third year of delinquency the state can auction a property. Check the state calendar for the next San Miguel County auction, which usually starts at 10:00 a.m.

How do I protest my San Miguel County property value?

Send the County Assessor a written petition by April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed, whichever is later. Explain the error and give your own figure.

Can I sell a San Miguel County house that has back taxes?

Yes. The closing pays the unpaid balance from your proceeds. Selling ahead of a state auction lets you control how it ends.

McKinley County in brief

Up in New Mexico's northwest, on the Arizona border, McKinley County has just one incorporated city, Gallup, which is also the seat. The 2020 census counted 72,902 residents, with 21,899 in Gallup and 2,900 in Crownpoint. That leaves 48,103 people spread across rural communities such as Thoreau, Tohatchi, Church Rock, Ramah, Pinehaven and Zuni Pueblo.

Over 60 percent of the county's land is part of the Navajo Nation or the Zuni Reservation. Median home value is $72,100, well under the state midpoint, so bills run smaller in dollars, though penalties work as they do elsewhere in the state. For most parcels, step one is learning which jurisdiction the land falls under.

Fee land, trust land and what you can sell

Land status decides which rules apply. Trust land inside the reservations is not subject to state or local taxes, though tribes may tax it to fund their own services. The Navajo Nation also levies a possessory interest tax on the right to use Navajo land for something like an oil and gas lease, a right-of-way or a business site lease. Fee land, ordinary privately owned land with a deed, stays under county rules.

  • Fee land with a recorded deed is assessed by the McKinley County Assessor and billed by the Treasurer.
  • Trust land and tribal land assignments follow tribal and federal procedures.
  • Before you price or advertise, find out whether your land is fee, trust, or held by lease or assignment.

The assessor's records and the county clerk's recorded documents are the quickest way to tell fee land from other holdings. A title company will ask the same thing first.

County offices

The McKinley County Assessor lists and values taxable property. The McKinley County Treasurer collects taxes, penalties and interest under the Property Tax Code, Sections 7-35-1 through 7-38-90 NMSA 1978.

OfficeWhat it doesHow to reach it

County AssessorDiscovers, lists and inventories taxable propertyAssessor page on the county site

The county posts charts of taxes billed by taxing entity for each tax year, which show how one bill divides among county, school and other districts. The county's treasurer and assessor pages are the place to begin.

Payment deadlines

McKinley County follows the statewide calendar, with payments due November 10 and April 10.

  • January 1: value is set for the year, and the tax lien attaches.
  • September 1: state finance officials set the rates.
  • November 1: bills go out.
  • November 10: first half due. Interest begins after December 10.
  • April 10: second half due. Interest begins after May 10.
  • January 10 of the next year: final day for a refund claim in district court.

Interest on late payments is 1 percent a month. Section 7-38-48 makes the tax a first lien that outranks every other interest, so an unpaid McKinley County bill stays with the house and lands on the next owner.

How your house is valued

As of January 1, the assessor puts a current and correct value on your home, and one third of that is taxable. A residential assessment may climb no more than 3 percent a year, unless ownership changes or the property is improved or rezoned.

Two things change at a sale. The cap lifts, so the buyer starts with a fresh valuation. The $2,000 head of family exemption, which covers a resident's primary home, is removed. Passing the home to a child who lives there, or into a revocable trust for a spouse or child, is not treated as a change of ownership.

How to appeal a high valuation

Your written petition must reach the assessor by April 1 or 30 days after the notice of valuation is mailed, whichever is later. The county valuation protest board decides it, and the state's Appraisal Bureau supplies one member.

A protest filed on time shields the disputed portion from delinquency. The other option is paying first and seeking a refund in district court. An initial protest costs nothing, and the state department publishes a protest pamphlet.

When the tax goes unpaid

Once three full years go by without payment, the account passes to the state's Delinquent Property Tax Bureau, which may sell the property at public auction. First it tries phone calls, certified mail, visits and notices left at the property, and it offers installment agreements.

Any auction proceeds beyond the tax, penalty, interest and costs go back to the former owner. Each county must have an auction every year, McKinley included.

  • Heirs of a house on fee land should review the treasurer's account first thing.
  • Owners who have moved away should make sure the treasurer holds a current mailing address.

How a quick sale usually goes

You show ownership, clear any tax lien and sign a deed, which the county clerk records. Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978 says an unrecorded deed has no effect on title against a later purchaser, and recording is how the buyer is protected.

When the house belongs to an estate, probate goes first. Real property rules out the small-estate affidavit, and a personal representative's deed may be what moves title from the decedent.

A sensible order is to confirm the land is fee land, get the treasurer's payoff, finish any probate step, then sign and record. A cash buyer closing as-is typically takes care of the rest. Before any of that, collect your deed, the latest tax bill and, for an inherited house, the estate papers, since the title company starts with those.

Timing a McKinley County sale around the tax year

When you sell matters less than whether the taxes are settled, but the calendar still shapes the paperwork. A sale in the spring, after the April 10 installment, usually means the current year is half paid. A sale in autumn may close before the bill even exists, since bills are mailed November 1.

Because the January 1 lien attaches no matter who owns the house later, buyers and title companies look at two numbers: what is owed from past years and what is owed for this one. Ask the treasurer for both, in writing if you can, and keep the answer with your closing papers.

If you are selling a rural home, ask the county clerk's office what is on record against it. A recorded deed, a clear chain of ownership and a paid-up treasurer's account are the three things a buyer will check. Owners of manufactured homes should also ask the assessor about the release before they list, since the home cannot be moved or retitled without one.

Finally, remember that the notice of valuation is not the bill. It arrives in spring, the bill arrives in November, and an unopened envelope in either month is the usual way a deadline is missed.

No. Trust land is not subject to state or local taxes. Tribes may assess their own taxes, such as the Navajo possessory interest tax.

The later of 30 days after the assessor mails the notice or April 1. The petition goes to the county assessor.

Yes. Because the lien outranks other interests, the tax must be paid or settled at closing. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure.
